# section: # generated from docs/CONFIG.md by tools/ci/config_table.py --import-page; edit this file, then --emit

meaning: Log file. An empty value writes no file.
Lowest level written: `error`, `warn`, `info`, `debug`, `trace`, or `0` to `4`. An unrecognised value keeps the level set in code.

default: Menu pointer debugging: `1` logs what the pointer hits and does, `2` also every widget it looks at, `3` also the parts of each button's box.
Logs every widget of each older GUI frame (pause screen, options, map) once: type, name, position, size and where the frame's camera puts it.

meaning: Heap section reserve in GiB, from 1 to 1024. Out of range: a warning is logged and 6 is used. Read only when `mem::Config.heap_reserve` is 0.

`auto`: the heap is a pagefile-backed section, except under Wine (Proton, SteamOS), where it is private memory: Wine backs sections with shared files and Linux GPU drivers import only anonymous memory, so with a section no memory pool reached the GPU (every draw read the dummy buffer: a black picture). `1`: always a section. `0`: always private memory (to try the Wine path on Windows). Without a section there are no alias views and no private views: pools import at their own address and `pool_mirror` is off.
Physical memory the process is told it has: GetInfo TotalMemorySize, and the ceiling of SetHeapSize together with the module images and 64 MiB.
Limit in GB for the process's host memory (private commit without the video memory the process has in use: Windows charges that to the commit too). Zero, negative or non-numeric: 8.
Memory guard poll interval in milliseconds. Zero or negative: 250.

Answer `is_mapped`, `protect` and the write tracker's arm (`src/mem/write_watch.cpp`) for ranges inside the heap view from a per-page table instead of `VirtualQuery` (which walks every page of the run on a section view: about 75 ms for a 3 GiB heap). `false` goes back to `VirtualQuery`; for before/after measurements. Read once.

Write tracking may cover the alias window where MapPhysicalMemory commits pages (nn::os VAMM, XC2 NS2's mesh pools), through each reservation's write-watch record. Off: those pages get no device-local copy. Read at start.

default: `main` (`present` for a game with `game::Info::present_interval_hz`: Fortune's Weave)
meaning: Where the frame limiter waits. `main`: at the game's frame boundary, before the input is sampled. The picture shown was simulated one render time earlier, not one queue depth earlier. `present`: inside the present call, as before. In both modes, a present that no boundary paced still waits in the present call. Read once.

`true` keeps the frame limiter's wait at the frame boundary while Reflex is on. By default Reflex's own sleep (minimum interval = the frame cap) paces the frame and the limiter waits only when Reflex is not active. Read once.

With vsync on and no frame cap below the display's refresh rate, the frame limiter holds 0.05% under the refresh rate so the swapchain queue stays empty (input to present p50 fell from 14 ms to 7 ms at 144 Hz in S21). `false` keeps the old behaviour: no cap, the display alone paces. Read once.

`nvnProgramSetShaders` returns success for a program whose shader block is missing from the shader cache (the program stays unlinked, its draws are skipped). `false` returns failure, which makes the game rebuild that shader on every bind. Read once.

A recording that runs out of the command or control memory the game added (the console usage is modelled per record) calls the game's command buffer memory callback, on the recording thread after the NVN call, so the game adds memory itself. `false` never calls it: such lists go in the buffer's overflow ring. Read once.

Import a memory pool for the GPU through a small private view of the heap section instead of the pool's own address in the multi-gigabyte primary view (tens of milliseconds per import against 0.05). `false` for before/after runs. Read once.

Also the launcher's and the F1 page's "Faster GPU memory" (`[display] fast_gpu_memory` in controls.ini), which applies when this key is not set. `on` (default): a memory pool that draws read vertices, indices or uniform blocks from gets a device-local copy, so draws stop reading host memory over PCIe. Pages are copied at the start of a submission after a draw wanted them; the CPU's writes are seen by page protection (`src/mem/write_watch.cpp`) and the GPU's by the replay, and a page that changed is read from the pool until it is copied again. A pool whose writes cannot be tracked (outside the heap's primary view, or `pool_view = false`) gets no copy. `off`: draws read the pools in host memory, as before. See `docs/S38.md`. Read once.

Compute results written into the pool copy stay there after their submission, their pages guarded (no access for the CPU): draws read the copy, other GPU readers get them copied back first, and the CPU's first touch (or nvnMemoryPool/BufferInvalidateMappedRange) copies them back on demand; pages the CPU read once go back at the end of every submission. `false`: every result goes back at the end of its submission and before any non-dispatch command (the old behaviour). Stats: the `compute out` line every 10 s.

A texture in a CPU_UNCACHED memory pool is written by the game without FlushMappedRange (the console's CPU writes are coherent). After its upload its storage pages are made read-only (`src/mem/write_watch.cpp`); at the start of each submission the pages the CPU wrote since count as flushed, and the textures there are uploaded again before their next use. ACNH's glyph cache needs it (new characters drew as nothing). `false`: off. Read once.

Most video memory the pool copies may take in all; a pool that would go over it stays in host memory. Not set: a quarter of the largest device-local heap, at most 8192 MiB, and no copies at all under 4 GiB of video memory. A value set here wins (0: no copies). The chosen cap is logged (`nvn.pool: pool copies: cap ...`). Read once.

With `[nvn] fb_debug = 1`: the fragment-shader hash prefix whose sampler bindings are reported ("17cdd28d" is the one HANDOVER 90 used). Empty reports every binding that ends up as a self-sampled attachment, capped at 500 lines.

Also the launcher's and the F1 page's "Fewer GPU pipeline waits" (`[display] fewer_gpu_waits` in controls.ini), which applies when this key is not set. `tracked` (default): a render pass that only wrote its attachments ends without a full barrier (the next pass that uses those images gets the barrier it needs), and image layout changes wait only for the stages of the old layout instead of all commands. `full`: a barrier on all commands and all memory after every pass, as before. Read once.

Measurement only. N > 0: `pool_mirror` and `pass_barriers` are off in even windows of N presents and as set in odd ones, so one run compares both (trace marks `gpuperf.on` / `gpuperf.off`). Read once.

Prepare the upload data of block-compressed textures (hash, BC7 cache read, untile) on worker threads as soon as the game initializes the texture, instead of on the render thread at its first use. A result is used only if no CPU write was reported since and the storage still hashes the same. `false` for before/after runs. Read once.
Worker threads for `tex_prep`; 0 is a third of the hardware threads, 2 to 8.
Most data, in MB, that finished or queued background results hold at once. Over it, the oldest unused results are dropped and the render thread prepares those textures itself.

Tests only: every Nth recorded submission and every Nth present throws `std::bad_alloc` on the render thread, to check that a failed render job costs one frame (an empty submission still signals its serial; the present counter is released) and nothing hangs. `0` = off.
Textures with less storage than this are prepared on the render thread (the hand-over costs more than the work).

Textures with at least this much storage are prepared as soon as they are registered in a texture pool (and, if sparse, after every batch of tile writes); smaller ones only when a command list binds their handle.
One log line per texture upload: format, size, and whether the data came from a background job or was prepared on the render thread, with the time spent.
Test aid: every background result is compared with a fresh preparation on the render thread; a difference is logged as an error and the fresh data is used.
Freeze threshold in seconds. Zero or negative disables the watchdog. Read only when the start call passes no value.
When the watchdog fires, wait this many seconds and dump every thread again if there is still no frame tick (a second sample tells a stalled thread from a busy one). 0 = one dump. The sweep sets 4.

Path of a file that receives one JSON line every `soak_interval_s` seconds for long-session monitoring: working set, private bytes, handles, threads, frame times of the window, and every gauge the runtime registers (live Vulkan objects, NVN objects, cache sizes, kernel tables, audio and movie queues). Empty: off, nothing runs. Read the file with `soak_report.py` (local test script).
Seconds between two lines of the soak file (0.5 or more).
`false` turns off the console core model.
Hexadecimal mask of host processors, intersected with the process affinity. Ignored when no bit matches. Empty: the runtime picks processors itself.

Which host processors the three console cores use when `host_cpus` is empty. `auto`: the three fastest free physical cores, one set per running nxrt process. `top`: the highest-numbered processors instead.

`nn::os::LockBusyMutex` runs as host code that gives the processor away while it waits (the SDK's loop is a pure spin and starved the lock holder under the console core model, debug note 240). `false` leaves the SDK code in charge.

Process priority class: `auto` (high when play mode has a window, otherwise left alone), `high`, `above_normal`, `normal`. The guest threads are pinned with the wake-up boost off, so under background CPU load a woken thread waits a scheduler quantum; see debug note 221.
The guest's `wfe` (and, every 64th time, `yield`) hand the host processor to another ready thread instead of spinning (debug note 420). `false`: a pause only.

A guest thread that stays ready without running (because other programs keep the host processor busy) is boosted to top priority for 450 ms, and its yields stop handing the processor over. See debug note 422.

A decal render query skips a model scene node that is already in the scene's lists but whose model data has not loaded yet, as the normal draw path does. Without it, such a node crashes the game in `CFrustumPlanes::BoxInFrustumPlanes` (S42). `false` runs the game's code unchanged, for reproducing the crash. Needs the hook sites in `main.sites`. Read once.

In the step where the jump timer ends partway, the jump force may raise the vertical speed only up to the rise cap, as on a fixed 1/60 step. Without it, a jump that is at the cap when its timer ends inside a long step goes up to about 6.9 x the step higher (+3.3 % with 16 ms frames; S49, S50). `false` runs the game's code unchanged. Needs the hook sites in `main.sites`. Read once.
How long a guest thread must stay ready and unscheduled before the guard boosts it, counted in 150 ms polls.
Seconds between log lines of per-thread kernel wait statistics (blocks per wait kind, time blocked, wake latency histogram, the thread's priority and core). `0` is off.

A guest thread about to sleep in WaitForAddress, ArbitrateLock or WaitProcessWideKeyAtomic first polls its wake flag this many microseconds with the kernel lock released. Off by default: in Dagsion 40 us caught 81 % of the main thread's waits but gave no fps (notes/perf.md).

Experiment: ArbitrateLock polls the mutex word this many microseconds before it queues as a waiter, and returns (the guest retries) when the owner releases it, so no hand-over to a sleeping thread happens. `0` is off. notes/threads.md.

Diagnostic: every nn::os::CreateThread, SetThreadName, SetThreadCoreMask, GetThreadAvailableCoreMask and GetCurrentCoreNumber call is logged (tag `threads`) with its arguments, the guest thread it made and the caller's guest backtrace. How a game sizes its thread pools (notes/threads.md).

Diagnostic, seconds between reports: how many threads of each named game pool (fefw: Basic_Worker, GFX_Worker, MOCull) are not blocked while main is blocked and while it runs (sampled every 250 us), which threads end main's waits and for how long it had waited, and kernel-lock contention. Guest threads take the game's names in the log while it is on. `0` is off.

Experiment: the number of cores the process is told it has (GetInfo CoreMask, valid core numbers), 1 to 16. Cores past the host's physical cores get SMT siblings as ideal processors. fefw does not size anything from it (notes/threads.md).

Experiment: `<return address>:<core>` (hex address): nn::os::GetCurrentCoreNumber called from there answers `<core>`. fefw `0x710197d0d8:5` gives its Basic job pool a fifth worker (no fps change, notes/threads.md).

Placement of the render thread (nvn-render): `off` leaves it to Windows; `core5` makes console core 5's processor its ideal one; `apart` also keeps it off main's physical core; a hex mask sets its affinity. No fps change measured (notes/threads.md).
Diagnostic: about 30 s in, one line with every registered thread's ideal processor and priority.

Joy-Con 2 mouse from the PC mouse (`docs/hid_mouse_sw2.md`). `off`: the game sees no Joy-Con 2 mouse. `on`: in play the mouse is never captured for the camera and always drives the Joy-Con 2 mouse. `auto`: the Joy-Con 2 mouse is on its surface whenever the camera does not hold the mouse (menus, `capture_mouse = false`, or the camera code yielding it).
Which input makes a mouse click: `both`, `device` (a real mouse) or `mouse` (the pointer only).

Result every stub-service command and every unknown command of a real service answers (logged at Warn once per command). `0` answers success with an empty reply (bring-up probe only: the guest then reads zeros and gets no objects). Pokopia does not need it: see IPC_ANSWERS.md.

Name prefix of the imports to log. Every call of an import whose name starts with it is logged in order (`hle-trace #n name(x0..x3) lr -> result`). Empty: off. Use it to see the order in which the game calls an API during start-up.
Number of traced calls logged before `hle` `trace` stops logging.
Each unknown SVC number is logged for its first N calls, then every 1000th call. Read on the first unknown SVC.
Seed for GetInfo RandomEntropy, subtypes 0 to 3.
Value returned by GetInfo SystemResourceSize.
Value returned by GetInfo ProgramId.
Process id returned by GetProcessId. The InitialProcessIdRange query uses the built-in `0x51` and ignores this key.
Host stack reservation per guest thread, in MiB. Values below 1: 64.
The uncaught-exception report calls `what()` of exception types derived from `std::exception` (a guest call). `false` prints the type only.

Vulkan device override: `discrete`, `integrated`, an index from the logged GPU list, or part of the device name. Empty: the discrete GPU with the most video memory, else integrated. A value that matches nothing is logged and the default is used.
Load VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation (with synchronization validation) and count what it reports. Needs the Vulkan SDK; without the layer a warning is logged and the run goes on.
No window and no surface: rendering goes to offscreen images (screenshots and automated tests).
Create the window hidden. CTest sets it to 1.

`fifo`, `fifo_relaxed`, `mailbox` or `immediate`. Wins over `[display] vsync` of controls.ini, which is where the mode came from before this key existed and which the launcher does not write: set, this key decides, otherwise vsync does. A mode the surface does not offer falls back (mailbox to immediate to fifo).
Frames the CPU may record ahead of the GPU, 1 to 3.
SDL scancode name of the key that shows and hides the ImGui overlay.

The pad chord that shows and hides the overlay: Switch buttons (after the player's mapping) joined by `+` (`a b x y l r zl zr plus minus up down left right lstick rstick`), `none` = no chord. The buttons of the press stay away from the game until released. While the overlay is up the pad drives its gamepad navigation (A activate, B back, d-pad or left stick move, L / R switch the menu's tabs) and the game gets no input.
Test aid: logs the F1 menu's gamepad cursor (focused item, popup) whenever it changes (notes/menu.md).
PNG path: the frame loop writes the presented image of `screenshot_frame` there.
Frame number captured when `screenshot` is set.
`1` writes one line a second with the presented frame rate and the GPU time of the present command buffer (output pass, FSR 1).

default: `high` (`fast` with the C++ build of bc7e)
meaning: How the game's ASTC textures reach this GPU (it cannot sample ASTC). `fast`: transcode to BC7 at the preset `[nvn] bc7_quality` (default 3) and cache it, as before; the default when the transcoder was built without ISPC (bc7e translated to C++, about 3 to 4 times slower; tools/textures/README.md). `high` (default with the ISPC build): the same at first, so nothing waits, then a background pool re-encodes each texture with bc7e preset 5 (`veryslow`; 3 with the C++ build; `[nvn] bc7_quality` when higher) and writes it to `bc7_cache` next to the fast entry; the next start finds it first and the texture is sharper for no frame cost. Fast entries (including the setup tool's BC5 and RGBA8 entries) keep working until a high one exists. `uncompressed`: every ASTC texture is decoded to RGBA8 (4 times the video memory of BC7, 4 to 16 times that of ASTC), the cache is not used, and the log gives the running estimate ("uncompressed ASTC textures so far ... MB as RGBA8 (BC7 would be ...)"). Applies at the next start; the F1 Graphics page and controls.ini `[display] astc_quality` set it unless this key is set. Sparse (virtual) textures keep their own transcode (`[nvn] sparse_bc7_quality`).
Below-normal-priority threads of the `high` background re-encode. `0` turns the re-encode off (the cache then stays at the fast preset).
Memory for the source snapshots of waiting and running re-encodes. A texture that does not fit is left for a later run.

Width of the window created at start. The window is the swapchain, so this is what the player sees; empty or 0 takes the display's size, because the game composes at 2160p docked whatever the window is (`switch2.cpp` `vi_query_buffer_max_resolution`), and a smaller window throws that composite away (HANDOVER 220).
Height of the window created at start; empty or 0 takes the display's size (HANDOVER 220).
With `[gfx] render_scale`: textures narrower than this keep their size. 0 = every qualifying texture scales. Read at start.
Calls of each unimplemented NVN entry point logged at Info; later calls are counted and logged at Trace.
Answer to an NVN name that is not in the table: `stub` hands out a logging stub (logged as UNKNOWN NVN PROC), `null` returns null.
Folder with `<code hash>.spv` and `results.tsv` (translated shaders). Empty: `./shader_cache/spirv`, then `shader_cache/spirv` beside the executable.

The preload pack `<shader_cache>.preload.pack` (`shader_cache/spirv.preload.pack`, beside the folder): the SPIR-V of the order file's (`[nvn] shader_order`) shaders in one zstd file (~1.1 GB -> ~290 MB), read front to back at boot instead of thousands of separate `.spv` files. Under Wine every file open goes through wineserver, and from a microSD card the separate reads ran at ~15 MB/s (Steam Deck boot shader wait 63 s -> ~11 s). The runtime writes it itself, in the background after a boot preload, when the pack lacks 32 or more of the order file's shaders (or 2%), as `.new`, which replaces the pack at the next start. Entries whose `results.tsv` line changed since (a shader translated again) are read from their `.spv` files. Logged as `nvn: shader pack: ...` and `shader preload: done after N s`. `0`: no pack is read or written. Read once.
Folder of ASTC to BC7 transcodes, keyed by a hash of the source bytes. Empty disables.

default: `3` (`1` with the C++ build of bc7e)
meaning: bc7e preset 0-6 for the fast transcodes done at run time, and the floor of the high preset (see `[gfx] astc_quality`). The transcoder built without ISPC starts at 1, about 3 times as fast as 3 and within 1.5 dB of it. The setup tool writes the value it was run with (default 3); `--quality 5` pre-builds the high entries.
bc7e preset 0-6 for textures the game module repaints (suit and arm cannon colour, S45). Lower is faster.

VkPipelineCache file, loaded with the first pipeline and written every 2 s while new pipelines appear (the prewarm's background thread does this, so only with `prewarm` on), and at shutdown. Empty disables.

Key file of the pipeline prewarm: every pipeline created at a draw is appended; the next run builds the recorded pipelines of a program on worker threads when the game sets its shaders. Empty disables the prewarm. Pipelines the key file does not know are linked from shader parts instead (`gpl`) and recorded here for the next run.
`false` turns the pipeline prewarm (recording and building ahead) off. The pipeline cache file is still used.
Worker threads that build recorded pipelines.

Link pipelines from separately compiled parts (VK_EXT_graphics_pipeline_library) when the key file has no pipeline for the draw. The shader parts of a program are compiled on background threads when the game sets its shaders. The draw links them together. Off, or on a GPU/driver without the extension: the whole pipeline is built at the draw as before.
Background threads that compile the shader parts.
Ask the driver to optimise the linked pipeline (costs more at the draw, keeps the optimisation data of every part in memory). For comparisons.

What replaces a pipeline that was linked from parts. `whole`: a background thread builds the whole pipeline from the same key and the next lookup swaps it in (the linked one is destroyed once the GPU is done with it). `lto`: the same thread links the parts again with link-time optimisation (about half the work; the parts keep their optimisation data). `off`: the linked pipeline stays. See `S29.md`.
Background threads that build the replacements.

Compile the shader parts of programs the game has set but not yet drawn with. This is a guess, and it avoids waiting at the first draw. `false`: only programs a command buffer was recorded with are compiled, a few frames ahead. About 10 times less compile work, at the cost of a wait of up to one part at the first draw of a new program.

Measurement only. N > 0 keeps the linked and the replacement pipeline of every draw and uses one or the other in alternating windows of N presents (log lines "ab: present ..."), so one run compares the two. Report: `gplopt_ab_report.py`.
Measurement only. N > 0: the compile threads rest in every other window of N presents. Slows loading (draws wait for parts); not for play.
Thread priority of the threads that build pipelines in the background (the prewarm and the shader-part threads): `below` (below normal), `normal`, `idle` (lowest).

Run the threads that build pipelines in the background in Windows efficiency mode (EcoQoS): on a CPU with fast and slow cores they go to the slow ones, so a burst of shader compiles does not take the fast cores from the game. The shader preparation always uses all the speed it can get.

Show a small 'Preparing shaders (N left)' note at the bottom of the screen while the background threads still have shader work queued for more than a second and a half; it stays up for one second after the queue empties. `false` keeps it off.

The shader preparation (`mpr.exe --prepare-shaders`, the launcher's Prepare shaders step) keeps what it compiled in the pipeline cache file (`pipeline_cache`; about 700 MB for the whole game). `false` keeps nothing: the preparation then only warms the graphics driver's own disk cache, which holds little of it. A cache file this big is read in one go at start and rewritten only after about 3,000 new pipelines.

Measurement only. Adds this text to every shader module as a source-extension string so the driver sees new shaders and compiles them from scratch, as on a player's first run, without touching the driver's cache on disk. Use a new text for every cold run.

Every translated shader stage reads its uniform buffers with robust access (`VK_EXT_pipeline_robustness`; robustBufferAccess2 where the GPU has it): a read past a block's bound size gives zero, as the console's constant buffers do, instead of reading whatever lies there (Fortune's Weave's lighting compute shaders index past theirs). Storage buffers, vertex input and images keep the device default. `false` turns it off (to measure its cost). Logged as `uboRobustness` in the device features line.

A memory pool larger than one chunk is imported into Vulkan (`VK_EXT_external_memory_host`) in chunks of this many MiB, each with a quarter of it more overlapping the next chunk (a binding up to that long always lies in one chunk), on the render thread the first time a draw, copy or texture touches it; it is not prefetched whole. Rounded up to a multiple of 64. Each import pins its pages (about 0.25 ms per MiB) and a `vkQueueSubmit2` running beside it waits, so a whole 3500 MiB pool cost ~0.9 s while draws read a few MiB of it. A longer range that crosses a chunk boundary gets one more import over the chunks it touches (`nvn.pool: ... span import`). Pools no larger than one chunk are imported whole in the background, as before. `0`: every pool is imported whole (before/after runs). Read once.

A texture whose storage does not lie inside its memory pool (placed past the pool's end, or at offset -1 when the game's allocator found no room) in a pool the CPU cannot access (`CPU_NO_ACCESS`: render targets, shadow maps, window textures) gets GPU memory of its own: its Vulkan image is the texture, with no bytes in the game's memory (nothing to upload, nothing to read back; the image starts cleared). Texture objects over the same pool and offset share one image (at offset -1 they cannot: that names no storage). Textures in pools the CPU can access and buffer textures (their texels are read from the pool's memory) are still refused (`nvnTextureInitialize: ... not host-backed`). The first 16 such textures are logged; gauges `nvn.textures_overflow`, `nvn.textures_overflow.bytes`. `0`: every such texture is refused (as before). Read once.
Import a memory pool into Vulkan on a background thread when a buffer is created over it, instead of on the render thread at the first draw.
Folder that `shot_frames` writes to, relative to the working directory.

Presented frames to save as PNG, counted from 1: a comma list of numbers and `from:to:step` ranges (e.g. `300,1000:2000:50`). Files are `<shot_dir>/<number, 6 digits>.png`. Lets a run be compared frame by frame with a reference capture.

For a game that paces itself by the console's vsync and steps its logic by a fixed amount per frame: the frame limiter holds it to this rate divided by the NVN window's present interval (`nvnWindowSetPresentInterval`; 60 / 2 = 30 fps), on top of `[display] fps_limit`, whatever the host display's refresh rate and vsync. `0` ignores the interval (the game then runs as fast as the limit allows, and too fast). Interval 0 sets no rate.

Frame pacing record: one line per present (number, the time it left the frame limiter, the time its present call returned, the limiter's wait, the game's rate). Time 0 is the log line `frame csv ...: its time 0`. Window runs only (a headless run has no limiter).
Folder that receives every shader block the shader cache has no translation for, as `code_<hash>.bin`, `ctrl_<hash>.bin` and `manifest.tsv`, for `spirv_harness --batch`. Empty: off.

Debug: comma list of vertex-shader hash prefixes. Every replayed draw with one of them is logged at Info under `nvn.drawlog`: presented frame, vertex count, instance count and the vertex stage's first four uniform blocks. Empty: off.

Debug: a 6-vertex instanced draw whose instance count changed logs the guest's frame-pointer backtrace (`nvn.drawbt`, 60 lines at most) and publishes the ui2d TextBox being drawn for `[fefw] tw_probe_watch = 2` (notes/fps120.md).

Presented frame number, or a comma list (`6050` or `6050,9300`). Every draw, clear, copy and dispatch of a traced frame is logged at Info under `nvn.trace`: programs, render targets, sampled textures, blend and depth state.

Hash prefix of a fragment shader. The frame after the first one that draws with that shader is traced, so the trace follows the scene rather than a frame number (which differs between runs). Only fires after `trace_min_sec`.
Seconds after the first draw before `trace_after_fs` can fire.
Traces the first frame presented this many seconds after the game submits its first frame. `0`: off.
Folder for the textures a traced frame samples: the texture data as prepared for the GPU, and the raw level 0 as the GPU holds it (`gpu_t<id>.bin`), to compare the two. Empty: off.
Draw numbers of the traced frame, a comma list (`253,300`). After each of those draws the colour and depth targets are copied to `snap_d<draw>_t<id>_<format>.png`.
Comma list of fragment-shader hash prefixes. Every draw of the traced frame whose fragment shader hash starts with one of them is snapped, as `trace_snap` does.
`1`: a snapshot draw also copies the textures that draw samples.

Comma list of compute-shader hash prefixes. After every dispatch of the traced frame with one of them, the textures and images it binds are copied to `snap_c<dispatch>_<hash>_t<id>_<format>.png` (float formats also as `.png.bin`, the texel bytes).
`1`: logs the life of the 128 x 128 textures with six layers and eight levels at Info under `nvn.tev`: creation, CPU writes, uploads and copies.

Every GPU access to a mirrored pool goes through its device-local copy; the CPU's writes are captured at each submit call, so the GPU reads the bytes of that moment (the flashes and flicker on NVIDIA). One copy per pool. `auto`: on when the copies' budget (`pool_mirror_mb`) is at least 3584 MiB. Read at start.

With `mirror_capture`: where the CPU's writes are captured. `submit`: on the game thread at the submit call; `replay`: when the render thread replays the submission (cheaper for the game thread, but the GPU can see newer bytes). Read at start.
Pages a mirror copies, and pool reads that have no copy, are snapshotted from game memory at replay into upload memory instead of read by the GPU live. Read at start.
Big pools without a private view are imported in chunks too. Read at start.
Pools flagged SHADER_CODE get a device-local copy (XC2 NS2 keeps its mesh data in 500-640 MiB SHADER_CODE pools). Read at start.
Pools imported at their own address in the alias window (MapPhysicalMemory pages) get a device-local copy, tracked by `[memory] vamm_write_watch`. Read at start.
Every pool the GPU can reach is imported in the background as soon as it is created, not at its first draw. Read at start.
Per-instance vertex streams are snapshotted per draw. `auto`: off while `mirror_capture` is on (the streams already read the captured copy). Read at start.
Switch 2: queue fences and window-acquire syncs wait for the queue's own work. `false`: for every queue's newest work (the Switch 1 behaviour) - slower, the safe fallback on NVIDIA. Read at start.
Textures whose background preparation finished are uploaded at the start of a submission, outside the render passes. Off: it uploaded in bursts during play. Read at start.
A texture's first upload goes into a command buffer that runs before its submission (Frame::prologue), so the render pass need not end for it. Read at start.

Frame trace file: zones of the render path, slow SVCs and slow HLE calls with their threads and times, flushed once a second. Analyse with `scripts/prof/ftrace_report.py`. Empty: off (one relaxed load per zone).
Size of the event array (24 bytes each, allocated when the trace starts); events past it are dropped.

With a trace on: when no frame was presented for this many milliseconds, dump every thread's stack to `<trace>.stacks` (up to four times per stall) and, when the stall ends, the CPU time each thread used in it. Analyse with `scripts/prof/stack_report.py`.

Sampling profiler for machines without a profiler that can run unelevated: that many times a second every registered thread is stopped briefly and its host stack read; each sample is weighted by the CPU cycles the thread used since its last sample. `0` is off (maximum 2000). The result is written at shutdown to `sample_out`.

Folded stacks of the sampling profiler (`label;thread;outermost;...;leaf kilocycles`, one per sample; the label is the scene a test script marked with `@log SCENE start NAME`). `prof_report.py` turns it into tables.
Comma-separated symbols whose frames the sampling profiler names `symbol+0x<offset>` (instruction-level hot spots of a few functions).

With the frame trace on: GPU timestamps between the render passes of every submission. The trace gets one event `gp:<label>` per interval (`gap`: copies, dispatches and barriers between passes, `pass WxH cN:fmt dfmt`: one render pass, with the draw count as argument, `tail`) so the GPU time can be added up per pass kind. Costs a pipeline drain per timestamp: for profiling only. `scene_report.py --gpu` prints the table.
Output size as `WIDTHxHEIGHT`, e.g. `1280x720`. Empty or not parseable: the default for the operation mode.
`handheld` sets handheld mode. Any other value is docked.

When set, the software keyboard applet (a game asking for a name or other text) answers this text at once, without asking anyone (test runs). Unset: the on-screen keyboard asks, or the game's initial text is answered when it is off.

The software keyboard asks the player on an on-screen keyboard drawn by the F1 overlay inside the game window (no second window): header and guide text from the game, the text field (masked for passwords, limited to the game's maximum length in characters), OK and Cancel. Typing on the keyboard, clicking its keys with the mouse and walking its key grid with a pad (d-pad or left stick; A types the key, B deletes, Y space, X shift, L/R move the caret, + OK, - cancel; the help line names the buttons by label or by position after `[pad] label_abxy`) all work; Enter answers, Escape cancels. The game waits for the answer and presents no frames meanwhile, so the runtime pumps the window, reads the pads and shows the last frame again with the keyboard on top from the blocked window thread (`kernel::set_blocked_hook`). Needs a game window and the overlay. `false`: never ask, the game's initial text is answered (or `Player`). `force`: also without a window, creating the overlay for it (scripted headless runs).

Switch 2 graphics scaling answer (`GetGraphicsScalingParameters`): `10` is scale level 0, the console's full-quality one; `20` and `30` are levels 1 and 2. Pokopia's dynamic resolution tops out at 1920x1080 at level 0 docked, 1728x972 at level 1 and 1664x936 at level 2.

Pokopia: `switch2`, `high` or `ultra`. When set, wins over the F1 page at start and after every settings change: view distance x1 / x1.5 / x2, texture LOD bias 0 / -0.5 / -1.0, anisotropy game / 8 / 16.

Pokopia: multiplier on the camera's far clip, 1.0 to 4.0 (1 = the console's). When set, wins over the F1 page and the preset. Applied in KTGL's projection builder (mid hook 0x7101f12130) to perspective cameras wider than 1.2:1, at each camera's next projection rebuild.

Pokopia, experimental: `1` writes the engine's camera TAA enable (and a jitter pattern of 8 when the game's is below 2) before the game reads it, which turns on the engine's projection jitter (mid hooks 0x7102126a88, 0x7102574a18); `2` also sets the TemporalAA3 pass switch at each of its render calls (entry hook 0x7101e5389c). Needs the lifted libs with those sites. Off by default: whether the game then builds its TAA pass and a velocity target is not confirmed. The probe logs the game's own values (`taa:` lines) either way. Read at start.

Pokopia: multiplier on the distance where placed objects switch to their low-detail model, 0.25 to 8 (1 = the console's: 3000/4500 units in the first area). Unset, it follows the view distance (presets x1 / x1.5 / x2). Applied at the placed-object update (mid hooks 0x71008f3a20, 0x71008f3fa0).

Pokopia: multiplier on the amount of each of the three height-fog layers (fragment shader 7c8c05da24a1f5a2, uniform block 3, c3[0..2].w), 0 to 1.5 (1 = the console, 0 = no height fog). The shader clamps each amount to 1, so values above 1 only raise layers below full strength. The game's memory is not changed: the NVN back end binds a scaled copy of the block. Read at start.
Pokopia: render the scene at the chosen internal size instead of the game's 1920x1080 layout. 0 = the game's layout.

Pokopia: the mouse pointer also works in menus opened during play (bag, lists, choices): left click confirms the selected entry, the wheel moves the selection, mouse look pauses while one is up. Detection: a cursor and a list of 2+ entries in layouts the game drew this frame (pane draw hooks). 0 = menus out of play only.
Pokopia: layouts (`id/sub id/sub ...`, as the `in-game menu up` log line names them) never treated as a menu.

Fortune's Weave: `1` makes the game's frame rate target 60 where it stores 30 (main 0x7bf1c0, an inline site in `recomp/games/fefw/main.sites`), so gameplay runs at 60 fps: the logic steps by 60 / target and the present interval follows it, as with the IPS that patches `mov w9, #30`. Text that types per frame types twice as fast (notes/pacing.md). Read at start.

Fortune's Weave: `1` runs gameplay at 120 fps at the right speed (wins over `fps60`): at the same site the game's display rate becomes 120 with the target, so its step is 60 / 120 and menus keep 60; the runtime's present rate follows (`nxrt::set_present_interval_hz`). Needs `[display] fps_limit` 0, auto or at least 120. Frame-counted effects (the dialogue typewriter) run 4x. notes/fps120.md. Read at start.

Fortune's Weave: the game's time step plus a quarter of the time it still owes (measured minus stepped), at an inline site in its step (main 0x180ef44). The game's own rule (a whole 60 / target per frame unless the frame took that plus 0.1) runs about 7 % slow at 120 near 110 fps, and at 60 drifts when frames are uneven or 1.0-1.1 steps long. With this the clock is exact and the steps stay the game's own where they are even. Frames over 8 steps (loads) keep the game's rule. Default: on with `fps120`, off otherwise. `[fefw] step_csv = <file>` logs every step (debug). notes/fps120.md. Read at start.

Fortune's Weave, debug: at this many seconds after play mode starts, find the objects whose vtables `[fefw] tw_probe_vt` lists (hex module offsets, default nn::ui2d::TextBox and ui::control::TextBoxEx) in the guest heap, sample them and what they point to every 2 ms for `[fefw] tw_probe_ms` (default 4000), and log the words that change step by step. `[fefw] tw_probe_watch` = 1 or 2 (2 needs `[nvn] draw_bt`) and `[fefw] tw_probe_off` instead write-protect one field of the dialogue's TextBox and log every write (host function, guest function, x30). Used to hunt the dialogue typewriter (notes/fps120.md). `0` = off.

Fortune's Weave: every this many seconds, log how fast the game's own clock ran against real time (its time manager, `1.000x` is the right speed), with the target frame rate and the last step. `0` = off. The F1 menu (Debug tab) changes it live and shows the clock's rate over the last 5 s whatever the period.

Fortune's Weave: the game's output size (its DLSS output, UI and post effects): `console` (the render config the game picks: docked 2560x1440, handheld 1920x1080), `720p`, `1080p`, `1440p`, `2160p` (or `4k`), `window` (the window's client size at start, fitted to 16:9) or `WxH`. At most 3840x2160 (the game's window textures). The game builds its targets once, so it applies at the next start. Above 1440p the window needs a 2160p display answer (`[vi] buffer_max_resolution` 3, the docked default). notes/resolution.md.

Fortune's Weave: the render (internal) size as a fraction of the output per side, 0.25 to 1.0; `0` keeps the game's own (0.5). `1.0` renders at the output size (the upscaler then only anti-aliases, as DLAA).
Fortune's Weave: a fixed render size `WxH` (at most the output); wins over `render_ratio`.
Fortune's Weave: the shadow-map base size, 512 to 8192; `0` keeps the config's (2048 docked, 1536 handheld).

Fortune's Weave: room past the game's 1008 MiB render-target pool, 0 to 3072 MiB. When the pool's allocator (an `nn::mem::NumberLineAllocator`) finds no room, the host places the target at an offset past the pool instead (from 1 GiB on, first fit; freed places are reused), and the back end gives it GPU memory of its own (`[nvn] texture_overflow`). What fits in the pool is placed as before. Needed by 4096 or 8192 shadows with some render sizes, and by a 2160p output rendered above half per side (2160p native with 8192 shadows uses about 2.1 GiB of it). Only what overflows costs GPU memory; the log says `render-target pool full: ... placed past it`. `0`: off: such targets get offset -1 from the game's allocator, and above 1440p output the render is capped at half per side. Read at start.
Fortune's Weave: `docked` gives every render config the docked config's quality settings (shadows and the handheld reductions), so handheld mode or a 1080p display answer keep them.

Fortune's Weave: the button glyphs in the game's text (A, B, X, Y, L, R, ZL, ZR, +, - and the face-button position dots) follow `[prompts] style` in `controls.ini`: PlayStation, Xbox or keyboard keys, or the game's own Switch glyphs. Drawn into the game's extension-font sheets, live. `0` leaves the game's glyphs alone. Read at start. notes/prompts.md.
Fortune's Weave, debug: a folder where every glyph cell drawn (and the game's originals) is written as a `.pgm`.

`auto` plays through XAudio2 on the default output device and falls back to the null sink (no sound, a warning in the log) when XAudio2 or a device is missing. `xaudio2` is the same with an explicit name. `paced` is a simulated device: it drains its queue at the sample rate and reports underruns and queue levels, which is how the renderer's timing is checked on a machine without a sound card. `null` discards everything. Tests install their own sink.
Clock error of the paced sink in parts per million (positive: the simulated device runs fast). Used to check that the renderer follows a device clock that is not exactly the host's.

`mf`: the game's `movie::` imports (Extractor, Decoder, MediaData, Buffer) are answered on Windows Media Foundation. `off`: the library compiled into subsdk0 runs (it needs the NVDEC/VIC driver, which does not exist here, so no movie plays).
One log line per sample read and per input buffer sent to a decoder. Very verbose.

When the game has selected every audio and video track of a movie, `SelectTrack` waits (at most 2 s) for the first decoded samples, on the thread that sets the movie up, so the main thread's first `GetSampleTime` does not wait for the decoder to start.

Switch 2 titles with `game::Info::movie_video_decoder` (Fortune's Weave): `host` decodes AV1 with dav1d into the player's CPU frames; `skip` makes every movie fail to open, and the game moves on as after a skip.

What `nn::vi::QueryDisplayBufferMaxResolution` answers (0 720p, 1 1080p, 2 1440p, 3 2160p). Fortune's Weave picks its render size from it: 3 renders 1280x720 into 2560x1440, 0 its lowest config (640x360 into 1280x720).
When every selected track reaches its end, the reader is positioned at the start and the first samples are decoded ahead, so `SeekTo(0)` of a looping movie swaps them in at once.
The extractor destructor returns at once; a short-lived thread joins the reader thread and releases the Media Foundation objects (60 to 80 ms on the calling thread otherwise).
`library` decodes VP9/VP8/AV1 on the host, `guest` leaves it to the game's own code, `off` disables video.
Decoder threads, clamped to 1..16; 0 means half the cores (the 4K AV1 files need the room).
Keep the player's timer alive while a movie runs; without it the picture freezes for seconds (handover 181).
Audio/video offset handed to the player, in milliseconds: this is the XAudio2 queue plus the device buffer on this machine.

Decode the film's own audio track on the host. Keep 0: in these containers that track is a placeholder and every packet carries one byte (ffprobe on `stream/movie/*.webm`, 2026-11-21: 200 packets, size 1, timestamps matching the runtime's), so the host decoder has nothing to decode. A film's sound comes from `stream/cs/<language>/<id>.nop` through the game's own audio system. Requires a runtime built with libvorbis (`NXRT_HAVE_VORBIS=1`).
Take movie timestamps from the host clock instead of the game's tick (debugging aid).

Hardware decoding of the movie's VP8/VP9/AV1 through FFmpeg libavcodec on the GPU (D3D11VA); off keeps libvpx/dav1d on the CPU. The 4K AV1 openings decode at 30 fps with it (dav1d: 8-17 on the same machine). On by default since 0.1.4: the cutscene audio race that made it unusable is fixed. A GPU without the hardware decoder falls back to the CPU decoders on its own.
Path of a 16-bit PCM WAV file that receives every frame the game sends to the host sink. Empty: no file. See the audio notes below.

Master volume, from `0.0` (silent) to `1.0`. Values outside that range are clamped. Applied by the XAudio2 sink. The F1 settings menu's Audio page edits the same value in `controls.ini` (`[audio] volume`), which applies when this key and `NXRT_AUDIO_VOLUME` are not set.

Output device for the XAudio2 sink: `default`, an endpoint id, or part of a device's name. See the audio notes below. The Audio page of the F1 menu writes `[audio] device` in `controls.ini`; it applies when this key is not set, at the next start.
Channel count the game's audio renderer works with: `6` for 5.1, any other value for stereo.

audout (the PCM output stream games like Pokopia mix into): how far ahead of the device's play position a buffer is handed back to the game, in ms (0 to 200). The device then always holds the game's own queue plus this margin, so it never runs dry between two game buffers; more is safer against stalls, less is lower latency. Only applies to a sink with a device clock (XAudio2, `paced`). Read once.
Seconds between the periodic sink stats lines in the log (queue depth average and min..max in ms, underruns, drops, frames/s the game delivered). `0`: off.
Title id of the game. `[process] program_id`, when set, overrides it. Also the default for `save_owner_id`.
Title name in the control data.
Display version string in the control data.
Comma list of language names (e.g. `AmericanEnglish,Japanese`), or a hex or decimal mask. Empty, or a list that names no language: the default.
Owner id of the title's save data. Unset, it follows the program id.
Account save data size, in bytes.
Account save data journal size, in bytes.
Device save data size, in bytes. `0`: none.
Device save data journal size, in bytes. `0`: none.
Cache save data size, in bytes. `0`: none.
Cache save data journal size, in bytes. `0`: none.
Main thread stack size, in bytes (main.npdm).
Main thread priority (main.npdm).
Main thread processor number (main.npdm).

Console language by name, e.g. `Japanese`. `auto` or empty: the player's pick in controls.ini (`[tweaks] language`, set in the launcher), else the Windows display language. A language the title lacks falls to its nearest sibling (British for American English, and so on), else American English. The log says which language was used and where it came from.
Region by name (`Japan`, `USA`, `Europe`, `Australia`, `HongKongTaiwanKorea`, `China`) or number (Japan 0 to China 5). Empty: USA.
Firmware version that `set:sys` GetFirmwareVersion reports.
Console nickname.
Nickname of the local user.
Local user id as 32 hex digits. Anything that is not 32 hex digits keeps the default.
Host folder served as the game's RomFS, relative to the working directory.
Folder for save data. Empty: the APPDATA default.
fefw.exe: the ExeFS folder the six NSOs are mapped from (`--exefs` sets it too).
fefw.exe: main as an uncompressed NSO (the console's main is ZBIC-compressed, which the NSO loader cannot read; fefw.exe refuses it). Empty: `<exefs>\main`. `--main` sets it too.
A folder whose contents overlay the romfs; empty or missing means no mods.

Folder the game's photos (caps:su SaveScreenShotEx0/1/2) are written to, one PNG per photo named by the local date and time (`YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS-mmm.png`). A relative path is taken from the exe's folder. Created when the first photo is saved.
Fatal-error report file. Once the key is set, even to empty, its value is used. Empty: no file is written.
`true` ends the process with exit code 5 after a fatal report. `false` returns.
`true`: no connection, no friends and no BCAT data (the start-up log line says so).
Folder searched first for `DejaVuSans.ttf` and the shared font dumps. Empty: the search goes on to `fonts\` next to the exe, then `assets\fonts\` under the working directory, then the exe's folder.
Settings file of play mode (controls, sensitivity, display); written with the factory settings when missing.
Capture the pointer (relative mode) while the game is in play.
Pitch limit of the mouse aim in degrees; 0 uses the game's tweak value.
Closing the window ends the process.
Base of the game's main module (hook addresses).
One status line per second in the log.
Test aid: draws an arrow at the menu pointer into the game's own frame, so a game screenshot shows where the pointer is (the OS cursor is not part of the frame).
Window self-test script for the oracles (steps are listed in that header).
Pump the window's events again right before the first `ProcessInput` of a frame takes the mouse counts, so the aim includes what the mouse did since the frame boundary.

Button icons the game's prompts show. `auto` (the default) shows keyboard and mouse icons until a controller is used, then that controller's icons, and goes back to the keyboard when a key or mouse button is pressed. The other values are `switch` (the game's own icons), `xbox`, `playstation` and `keyboard` (keyboard and mouse). Also accepts `ps`, `ps4`, `ps5`, `dualsense`, `kbm`, `mouse` and `keyboard_mouse`. Stored in `controls.ini` under `[prompts]`, not in `nxrt.ini`. Set it in the launcher (Controls tab) or on the F1 page (Controller tab, Button prompts). Changes apply on the next frame, with no restart. Keyboard icons show the keys the action is bound to: a rebound jump key shows the new key, and a key with no icon of its own gets a plain key icon. Xbox and PlayStation icons follow `[padmap]`.

Frame rate counter in a corner of the game window. Off by default. While it is off, the overlay does one atomic read per frame and nothing else. The hotkey (`key`), the Display tab of the F1 page and the launcher's Extras tab can turn it on or off, and the choice is saved.
Keyboard key that shows and hides the counter. The game never receives it, so do not bind the same key to an action. Any SDL scancode name.
`top_left`, `top_right`, `bottom_left` or `bottom_right`.

`0` shows the frame rate only, `1` adds the frame time, and `2` also shows the 1% low (the frame rate of the slowest 1% of frames in the last 5 seconds) and the worst frame time in the last half second. The numbers refresh four times a second.

`0`: a frame being captured (the test tooling's `@shot`, `[nvn] shot_frames`, or the boot screenshots) is drawn without the counter. `1`: the counter appears in the picture. The self-test step `set:fps_in_shots=1` switches it.
`1` silences the game while its window has no focus (the master volume is kept). Live.
The display the window lives on: `auto` (where the window opens) or the display's number, 1 for the first in the system's order. Moves the window at once; a fullscreen window goes along.
The F1 menu's "Prepare shaders ahead": becomes `[nvn] prewarm` at the start unless that key is set in the ini or the environment.

The F1 menu's "Texture compression quality" (Graphics page, applies on restart): becomes `[gfx] astc_quality` at the start unless that key is set in the ini or the environment. `fast`, `high` or `uncompressed`.

What each controller button presses on the Switch pad. `default` keeps the built-in layout (`[pad] label_abxy` still decides the face buttons). `none` makes the button do nothing. Or list Switch buttons joined by `+` (`A`, `ZL+L`). Names describe position: `south` is the bottom face button (A on an Xbox pad, cross on a PlayStation pad). Stick directions are not allowed here. A remapped button stops pressing its built-in button.

Folder searched first for `prompt_icons.pak`, the button icon pack. Empty: the search goes on to `prompts` beside the executable, then `assets/prompts` under the working directory, then the executable's folder.

`auto`: a handheld when Steam sets `SteamDeck=1`, or the board's SMBIOS product name is Jupiter or Galileo (Steam Deck LCD / OLED) or its family starts with `Legion Go S`. The board is read from the registry (`HKLM\HARDWARE\DESCRIPTION\System\BIOS`, which Wine fills too), else from `Z:\sys\class\dmi\id` under Wine. Logged as `host: handheld: yes/no (why)`. On a handheld, `[display] render_scale` auto renders at the window's size instead of at least 1920x1080, and `[prompts] style` auto keeps the controller's prompts when the trackpad, touchscreen or on-screen keyboard send mouse or keyboard input. `on` / `off` force it either way (other handhelds: `on`). Read once.

Off by default since 0.1.4: the film overlay has no HDR10 encode yet, so a cutscene frame came out green on a display Windows reports as HDR; set `auto` (or use the launcher video page) after that is fixed. HDR output: `off`, `auto` (HDR when the display and Windows offer it), `on`, or `native` (as `on`, with the levels the game declares for an HDR TV on Switch 2: the `nn::vi` standard content luminance range is paper white unless `paper_white_nits` is set, the extended range or the NVN2 window content metadata is the content maximum in the swapchain's HDR metadata; NVN2 window colour space and HDR metadata calls are recorded too; one `HDR native:` log line gives the decision). Play mode reads the `[hdr]` section of `controls.ini` instead; this key only applies to code that does not load that file. The environment variable overrides the file in play mode. Applies at the next start.
Swapchain format: `auto` (HDR10 when offered, else scRGB), `hdr10` or `scrgb`. Same reading rules as `hdr` `mode`. Applies at the next start.
Peak brightness in nits: `0` takes the display's reported peak (1000 when it reports none), otherwise 200 to 10000. Same reading rules as `hdr` `mode`. Applies live.
Brightness of SDR white in nits: `0` takes Windows' SDR content brightness when HDR is on there (203 otherwise), otherwise 80 to 500. Same reading rules as `hdr` `mode`. Applies live.
How far highlights go above the game's own white: 0 keeps the SDR look, 1 lets them reach the peak, 2 is the most. Same reading rules as `hdr` `mode`. Applies live.

Colour controls of the present step: `neutral` (all four keys below at their neutral value) or `vivid` (contrast 1.1, saturation 1.15, black -0.03). Fills in the four keys; any of them set next to it wins. Play mode reads the `[picture]` section of `controls.ini` (which keeps the four values, not the preset); a `[picture]` key in mpr.ini or the environment replaces the file's four values. All neutral: the present is exactly the game's picture (the pass is skipped). Works on SDR, HDR and with FSR 1. Applies live (F1 Graphics page, Colour).
0.5 to 1.5: spreads the display-encoded signal away from mid grey (0.5). Same reading rules as `picture` `preset`.
0 to 2: colour intensity around the Rec. 709 luma (0 = grey). Same reading rules as `picture` `preset`.

-0.5 to 0.25: black level. Below 0 the signal at -black becomes black (crushes a lifted, hazy black); above 0 lifts black to this level. White stays. Applied first. Same reading rules as `picture` `preset`.

0.5 to 2: mid-tone brightness, signal^(1/gamma), applied last (above 1 brightens). Black and white stay. In HDR the four controls work on rgb^(1/2.2) of the scene-linear picture. Same reading rules as `picture` `preset`.

Upscaling: `off`, `fsr1` (AMD FSR 1; `spatial` is accepted as well) or `nis` (NVIDIA Image Scaling v1.0.3, any GPU; up to 2x per side, FSR 1 is used beyond that). Both upscale the picture when the render scale is below the window and the HDR scene when `scene_scale` is below 100. Temporal (`src/gfx/extras/temporal.cpp`, on the HDR scene before the tone map, with the scene depth, camera motion vectors made by the runtime and a sub-pixel jitter the runtime adds to the scene camera, see `jitter`): `fsr3` (AMD FSR 3.1 through the FidelityFX API, DLLs from `fsr_dll`), `dlss` (NVIDIA DLSS Super Resolution through Streamline, RTX GPUs, DLLs from `dlss_dll`; applies at the next start) and `dlaa` (DLSS at native size). `xess` is read and kept but runs as `off`. A temporal mode whose DLLs or GPU support are missing logs why and leaves the picture as `off`. Play mode reads the `[upscale]` section of `controls.ini` instead; the environment variable overrides the file. Applies live.

Render size preset of `fsr3` and `dlss`: `native` (100%, anti-aliasing only), `quality` (67%), `balanced` (59%), `performance` (50%), `ultra_performance` (33%) or `custom` (`scene_scale`). Takes effect only where the scene is rendered below the output size; Pokopia's scene renders at full size, so its temporal modes run at native size. Same reading rules as `upscale` `mode`.

With a temporal mode: `1` adds a Halton(2, 3) sub-pixel jitter (8 phases) to every scene camera block whose projection has none (the game's own TAA jitter never reaches its G-buffer camera); `0` never (debugging: no anti-aliasing gain). Read at start.
Debugging: flips the sign of the jitter handed to FSR 3 / DLSS (bit 0 x, bit 1 y). Read at the first temporal frame.
FSR 1, NIS or FSR 3 sharpening, 0 to 1 (1 is the sharpest; DLSS has none). Same reading rules as `upscale` `mode`. Applies live.

Percent of the output size per side that the 3D scene is rendered at, 25 to 100 (100 = off). The scene goes through the game's own dynamic-resolution path; the HUD and post effects stay at full size. Same reading rules as `upscale` `mode`. Applies live.

Path of the FidelityFX API DLL for `fsr3`: `amd_fidelityfx_loader_vk.dll` (FidelityFX SDK v2.4.0, 39 KB, with `amd_fidelityfx_upscaler_vk.dll` beside it), the v1.1.4 `amd_fidelityfx_vk.dll`, or `amd_fidelityfx_upscaler_vk.dll` on its own (36 MB; it exports the same `ffx*` entry points, measured 2026-11-19, so the loader is optional); empty means the first of these that exists: the loader, then `amd_fidelityfx_vk.dll`, then the upscaler, in `upscalers\\fsr3\\` next to the executable (the release package's folder), then in the executable's own folder. Kept verbatim. Same reading rules as `upscale` `mode`.

Folder (or the path of `sl.interposer.dll`) holding the Streamline DLLs for `dlss` / `dlaa`: `sl.interposer.dll`, `sl.common.dll`, `sl.dlss.dll` and `nvngx_dlss.dll` (Streamline v2.14.16 `bin/x64`), empty means `upscalers\streamline\` next to the executable when it holds `sl.interposer.dll` (the release package: the three Streamline DLLs are bundled, `nvngx_dlss.dll` is downloaded from NVIDIA by the launcher), else the executable's own folder. `real` mode: the step is never longer than 1/min_rate. A slower frame makes the game run in slow motion instead of taking one huge step.
`real` mode: the step is the mean of the last N frame times (1 = raw, 64 at most); a frame more than 50 % away from the mean restarts the window.
